procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dated 27.11.2002 rendered by the Sessions Court convicting Appellants-accused (A4 and A2) u/s.302, s.120B, IPC and sentenced accordingly.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Aggrieved by the Sessions Court order, the present appellants (A4 and A2), A3 and the State of Maharashtra preferred separate appeals before the High Court. The High Court dismissed all the appeals.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Aggrieved by the High Court's judgment, the appellants (A4 and A2) preferred appeals before the Supreme Court.

directions: The appellants are discharged from the liabilities of their bail bonds.
If any fine(s) pursuant to the orders of the Sessions Court or High Court were deposited by/realised from either appellant, they shall be entitled to refund of the same.

issue.issue_text: Whether High Court was justiﬁed in dismissing the appeals ﬁled by them and upholding their conviction.

facts: The appellants (A2 and A4) were not physically present at the scene of the crime, which was inside a car where the victim was shot.
The prosecution's case against the appellants was based on a theory of criminal conspiracy.
The alleged main conspirators and masterminds of the plot (A1 and A7) had already been acquitted.
The appellants were able to successfully challenge and 'poke holes' in the credibility of the testimonies of key prosecution witnesses (PW1, PW2, and PW7).
law: In criminal justice, a conviction cannot be sustained if there is a reasonable doubt as to the involvement of the accused in the crime.
The prosecution must prove its case, including any theory of conspiracy, beyond a reasonable doubt.
application: The Court found that the weaknesses in the testimonies of the prosecution witnesses created a reasonable doubt about the appellants' guilt.

The acquittal of the alleged main conspirators (A1 and A7) fatally undermined the prosecution's conspiracy theory. The Court reasoned that without the masterminds, the conspiracy angle against the remaining accused could not be considered proven beyond a reasonable doubt.

Since the appellants were not at the crime scene and no direct role was attributed to them, their conviction depended entirely on the conspiracy theory. With that theory having collapsed, their convictions became unsustainable.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that there was sufficient material on record to create a reasonable doubt about the appellants' involvement in the crime. The collapse of the prosecution's conspiracy theory, following the acquittal of the main conspirators, and the unreliable witness testimonies made the conviction unsustainable. Therefore, the Court held that the High Court was not justified in upholding the conviction, allowed the appeals, and acquitted the appellants.

arguments.issue_text: Whether High Court was justiﬁed in dismissing the appeals ﬁled by them and upholding their conviction.
appellant_arguments: The alleged rivalry between the deceased and the supposed masterminds (A1 and A7) was not proven, which is evidenced by the acquittal of A1 and A7.
There is no evidence connecting the money confiscated from A2's bank account and fixed deposit to the alleged masterminds (A1 and A7) or the conspiracy.
respondent_arguments: The Sessions Court's judgment, which was upheld by the High Court, should not be interfered with.
The Sessions Court clearly discussed the role of the appellants based on the testimony of witnesses.
The appellants were identified by prosecution witnesses.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: When a court is confronted with a situation where it must decide whether to lean towards the prosecution or the defence, in the face of reasonable doubt as to the version put forth by the prosecution, the court will, as a matter of course and judicial discretion, lean in favour of the defence.
obiter: Judgments are not to be read as Euclid’s theorems; they are not to be construed as statutes, and specific cases are authorities only for what they actually decide.
Life and liberty are not matters to be trifled with, and a conviction can only be sustained in the absence of reasonable doubt.
The presumption of innocence in favour of the accused and the insistence on the prosecution to prove its case beyond reasonable doubt originate from Articles 21 and 14 of the Constitution of India.
The presumption of innocence is a human right.
Liberty of a person should not ordinarily be interfered with unless there exist cogent grounds therefor.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: When the court is faced with a reasonable doubt regarding the prosecution's version of events, it must, as a matter of judicial discretion, lean in favor of the defense. A conviction can only be upheld if the prosecution proves its case beyond a reasonable doubt, as life and liberty are fundamental rights that cannot be trifled with.
legal_tests_applied: Proof Beyond Reasonable Doubt: The court applied the standard that a conviction requires the prosecution to prove guilt beyond a reasonable doubt. A reasonable doubt is defined as a fair doubt based on reason and common sense, arising from the evidence or lack thereof, as opposed to an imaginary, trivial, or merely possible doubt.

Presumption of Innocence: The court relied on the cardinal principle that an accused is presumed innocent until proven guilty, noting that this presumption is a human right and is traceable to Articles 14 and 21 of the Constitution.
policy_considerations: The presumption of innocence and the requirement for proof beyond reasonable doubt are not empty formalities; their origins are traceable to the fundamental rights to life and equality under Articles 21 and 14 of the Constitution of India.
A person has a profound right not to be convicted of an offense that is not established by the evidential standard of proof beyond reasonable doubt.
Life and liberty are not matters to be triﬂed with, and the liberty of a person should not ordinarily be interfered with unless there exist cogent grounds.
The presumption of innocence is a human right.
